title: Parameters from concentration versus time data

segs.text: Module two, objective three. Calculating parameters from concentration versus time data. Given a dose and one or two measured plasma concentrations, you find the patient's elimination rate constant k, the half-life, the concentration at time zero, C zero, the volume of distribution, the clearance, and amounts at stated times. The half-life is the time for the concentration or the amount to fall by half; for a first order drug it is the same at any level. Each value is used to find the next, so the order is k, then half-life, then C zero, then V D, then clearance and amounts.

card.m: given: D<sub>0</sub> and one or two C<sub>p</sub> values
t½ (hr): time to fall by half; the same at any level
k → t½ → C<sub>0</sub> → V<sub>D</sub> → Cl<sub>T</sub>, amounts

segs.text: Why does k come first? After a bolus the log of the concentration falls on a straight line, and k is the slope of that line with the sign changed, so any two points on the line give k. Two different pairs give nearly the same value. The two points must be of the same kind, two concentrations or two amounts. A dose in milligrams divided by a concentration in milligrams per liter leaves liters, not a fraction remaining, so it cannot give k. V D links the two kinds, because the amount equals V D times the concentration at the same time.

card.m: ln C<sub>p</sub> vs t: straight line, slope −k

segs.text: The relation is k equals l n C one minus l n C two, over t two minus t one: the drop in log concentration divided by the time between the samples. A larger drop over the same time gives a larger k. With amounts, k equals l n D zero minus l n D B, over t. The half-life equals zero point six nine three over k, which she expects memorised. k is on the bottom, so a larger k gives a shorter half-life, and per hour on the bottom leaves hours.

card.m: larger drop, same time → larger k

segs.text: C zero is rarely measured, because a sample cannot be drawn at the instant of injection, so the line is extended back to time zero: C zero equals C t times e to the k t. Going back in time makes the exponent positive, so C zero is higher than every sampled concentration. Then V D equals D zero over C zero, both at time zero, because the times must match, and clearance is k times V D. In the calculation clearance comes last, but in the body clearance and V D are what is set, and k follows from them. An amount at a later time is D zero times e to the minus k t, or V D times the concentration then; she accepts either.

card.m: +kt: back in time, C<sub>0</sub> above every sample
in the body: Cl and V<sub>D</sub> set, k = {{frac:Cl|V<sub>D</sub>}} follows
D<sub>B</sub> = D<sub>0</sub>e<sup>−kt</sup> or D<sub>B</sub> = V<sub>D</sub> × C<sub>t</sub>

segs.text: Her first practice problem gives two hundred milligrams by I V bolus to an eighty kilogram man, fifteen milligrams per liter at six hours, and a V D of ten percent of body weight. It asks the amount in the body at twelve hours and the half-life. The dose is an amount and the six hour value is a concentration, so one must be converted before k can be found. V D converts the concentration: ten percent of eighty kilograms, taking one liter as one kilogram, is eight liters, and eight liters times fifteen milligrams per liter is one hundred twenty milligrams in the body at six hours.

card.m: D<sub>0</sub> = 200 mg; 80 kg; C = 15 mg/L at 6 hr; V<sub>D</sub> = 10% of body weight
200 mg and 15 mg/L: not the same kind
DB = 8 L × 15 mg/L = 120 mg at 6 hr

segs.text: Two amounts now give k: two hundred milligrams at time zero and one hundred twenty at six hours, so k is zero point zero eight five per hour. The amount at twelve hours comes from D zero times e to the minus k t, and is seventy two milligrams. A check: zero point six of the drug remains after six hours, so after twelve hours zero point six of zero point six remains, and zero point three six of two hundred milligrams is seventy two. The half-life is eight point one five hours. Her added question asks the concentration at twelve hours: seventy two milligrams in eight liters is nine milligrams per liter. Read whether the question asks for an amount or a concentration.

Her exam one review problem gives a one hundred fifty four pound woman a fifteen milligram per kilogram I V bolus, with thirty two point eight five micrograms per milliliter at two hours and nine point three two at eight hours. Both values are concentrations, so k comes straight from them, zero point two one per hour, and the half-life is three point three hours. The dose needs the weight in kilograms, seventy, so the dose is one thousand fifty milligrams. Extending the line back two hours gives a C zero of fifty micrograms per milliliter, which is fifty milligrams per liter, since the two units give the same number. V D is twenty one liters, and clearance is four point four one liters per hour.

card.m: 154 lb; 15 mg/kg; 32.85 mcg/mL at 2 hr, 9.32 mcg/mL at 8 hr
{{frac:154 lb|2.2 lb/kg}} = 70 kg; D<sub>0</sub> = 15 mg/kg × 70 kg = 1050 mg

segs.text: Her questions run as one patient and a series of small parts, and on the exam an earlier part cannot be revisited. Weight in pounds with a milligram per kilogram dose tests the conversion of two point two pounds per kilogram, and every later part depends on it. Fifteen minutes is zero point two five hours. Ninety nine point nine percent eliminated means ten half-lives, because each half-life halves what is left. Keep k to three or four decimal places until the end, write a zero before a leading decimal point, and give units. The usual error is dividing the dose by a concentration to get k; convert one of them first.

card.m: k to 3 or 4 decimals; 0.21, not .21; units
